OTHER NOTES:

> Verify that the application protects against template injection attacks by not
allowing templates to be built based on untrusted input. Where there is no
alternative, any untrusted input being included dynamically during template
creation must be sanitized or strictly validated.

**"built"**
What does "built" mean? Many frameworks, templates are dynamic by nature.

**"sanitized" or "validated"**
Difficult to understand-- What is important and how -- is missing?

I think the sanitization should not be the primary defense in template engines, this is not same as HTML sanitization as far as I know and the requrement doesn't mention the insecure template engines.

comments.body:
I agree again that sanitization is not the right defense here - sanitizing data and then using is almost always a bad idea and validation/rejection cycles and normal JSON data flows to popular templates are better.

Perhaps:

_Verify that the application protects against template injection attacks by not allowing templates to be assembled based on untrusted input. Where there is no alternative, any untrusted input being included dynamically during template creation must be strictly validated._

We are rallying around sanitization (see #3335) so for uniform terminology I would say:

"_Verify that the application protects against template injection attacks by not allowing templates to be assembled based on untrusted input. Where there is no alternative, any untrusted input being included dynamically during template creation must be sanitized._"

> ... not allowing templates to be assembled based on untrusted input.

I don't think it is correct. It can be misinterpreted that you can not choose different parts of template based on user-input.

The point is - if template is **built** dynamically
* it must not contain user-controlled input
* OR the user-controlled input is validated or sanitized
I think the point is that the preference is not to use trusted input at all for templates

I would never use untrusted data - even sanitized data - to generate part of a _**template**_.

Half of the template is just static template data that is hard-coded by the dev, and then user data is dynamically loaded over JSON and rendered in specific slots meant for user data.

"sanitizing data and making it part of the template" (which is implied here) is not a good suggestion.

> I think the point is that the preference is not to use trusted input at all for templates

Good point, and I agree.

Just a note, if the requirement will contain "only validation is accepted", ~~the requirement needs to be moved to V1.2, and it is a breaking change~~ the requirement does not fit really well under the sanitization section title.
@jmanico what would your proposed alternative wording be?

I think we just need to stick with:

**_Verify that the application protects against template injection attacks by not allowing templates to be assembled based on untrusted input_**

And be done with it. There is no reason at all to use untrusted data as template code. At all.

> There is no reason at all to use untrusted data as template code. At all.

This can cause interesting "reports" that "I entered keyword-xyz and it was presented in the dynamically built template - so it is a problem".

Or... I entered "keyword-abc" and based on that, the template was assembled differently, so the "not allowing templates to be assembled based on untrusted input" is not met.

> > There is no reason at all to use untrusted data as template code. At all.
> 
> This can cause interesting "reports" that "I entered keyword-xyz and it was presented in the dynamically built template - so it is a problem".
> 
> Or... I entered "keyword-abc" and based on that, the template was assembled differently, so the "not allowing templates to be assembled based on untrusted input" is not met.

Perhaps more clear then:

_Verify that the application uses the templating engine’s variable-binding mechanisms to render untrusted input as data, and does not construct, modify, or evaluate templates (or template expressions) from untrusted input._

Before we settle on wording, I think there's a key design question to resolve first: should we remove the fallback entirely?

The current requirement has a two-tier structure: prefer not to use untrusted input in templates, but if you must, sanitize/validate. @jmanico's proposal removes that fallback, essentially saying there is never a reason to use untrusted data as template code.

I can see the argument for that, but are there legitimate cases where untrusted input does need to influence template structure (not just data rendering)? For example, CMS template customization, email template builders, or report generators where users configure layouts. If those cases exist, should we keep some kind of fallback?

@elarlang, @jmanico, what are your thoughts on this? Should it be an absolute prohibition, or do we need a "where there is no alternative" escape clause?

Once we've settled that, we can address the exact wording and also @elarlang's point about whether this requirement still fits under the Sanitization section.

Josh, I think this is a fair concern. But it's nearly impossible to sanitize untrusted templates.  Many template engines have multiple evaluation methods (expressions, filters, includes/imports, attribute access, function calls), so “validation” of template code easily misses real vulns. 

My take is:

1. For normal app templating, the requirement should read like an absolute prohibition: untrusted input may be data, never template code.
2. If the application intentionally provides template authoring, get ready for a very significant defense strategy that includes:

- a strict allowlist of functions/filters/tags (no arbitrary evaluation  (Twig)
- no access to filesystem, network, environment, process execution, or reflection (Jinja2, FreeMarker)
- no raw object graph traversal / attribute access unless explicitly allowed (Jinja2)
- resource limits (time/memory/recursion/output size) to prevent DoS (Twig)

@jmanico I think your proposal still contains an implicit escape clause. You say it should be an absolute prohibition, but then describe how template-authoring platforms should handle it with allowlists, sandboxing, and resource limits. That's effectively a "where there is no alternative" fallback, just described in more detail.

I think maybe the best approach is to keep the two-tier structure but raise the bar significantly for the fallback. The current "must be sanitized" might be problematic but if we acknowledge that template-authoring platforms (CMS systems, email template builders, report generators) are a real use case, we should describe what's actually needed.

Something like:

"_Verify that the application protects against template injection attacks by not allowing templates to be assembled based on untrusted input. Where this is absolutely necessary, the application must ensure that untrusted template code is evaluated with only the minimum necessary functionality enabled and cannot be used to access application internals or server resources._"

The first sentence keeps the original structure (with "assembled" replacing "built" for clarity). The second sentence replaces "sanitize" with a goal-focused statement that captures both the need to restrict the template engine's own capabilities (your allowlisting point) and the need to prevent breakout to the server environment.

We then need to think about section placement...
I think this is a great solution Josh. Nice work. 🤙
@elarlang any further thoughts on the proposal?

> “minimum necessary functionality”

What does that mean? 
How verifier/developer can decide?

> Application internals or server resources

This is incomplete, because template injection attacks often lead to more than just resource access.

> "assembled based on untrusted input"

This is ambiguous.


it's good to add into the requirement text - "**template engine’s data-binding mechanisms**"

@ajayojha thanks for the feedback, let me address each point:

**"minimum necessary functionality"**: Clearly we cannot cover every eventuallity but like (for example) "the principle of least privilege", it is intended to make clear that all functionality provided to the template evaluation context needs to have a valid reason. I think this is a well-understood security principle but open to suggestions if you think there is a clearer way to express it.

**"application internals or server resources"**: How would you expand this list?

**"assembled based on untrusted input"**: I could change this to "manually assembled based on untrusted input" to make it clearer that we are talking about programmatic construction of template strings from user input, not simply selecting which template to display.

**"template engine's data-binding mechanisms"**: This is an interesting suggestion (and one @jmanico also proposed earlier). The question is whether we want the requirement to prescribe the mechanism (use data-binding) or just prohibit the dangerous practice (don't assemble templates from untrusted input). I think there is value in mentioning it as the expected approach. Perhaps the first clause could become something like:

"_Verify that the application protects against template injection attacks by using the template engine's data-binding mechanisms for untrusted input and not allowing templates to be manually assembled based on untrusted input._"

Combined with the updated fallback, the full requirement would be:

"_Verify that the application protects against template injection attacks by using the template engine's data-binding mechanisms for untrusted input and not allowing templates to be manually assembled based on untrusted input. Where template authoring by users is an intentional feature, the application must ensure that untrusted template code is evaluated with only the minimum necessary functionality enabled and cannot be used to execute arbitrary code or access application internals or server resources._"

Thoughts from @ajayojha, @jmanico, @elarlang?

Do we need the 2nd part of the requirement? If yes, then we need to add a similar "disclaimer" also, for example, to the WYSIWYG requirements that says that for admin purposes, users with necessary privileges can enter scripts and so on. I would not like to go there.

Also, the 2nd part goes to the configuration area and duplicates the requirement 13.2.2:
> Verify that communications between backend application components, including local or operating system services, APIs, middleware, and data layers, are performed with accounts assigned the least necessary privileges.
